learn.title: Microgrids for Energy Independence
learn.intro: Microgrids are localized energy networks that can operate independently from the main grid, offering villages energy independence and critical resilience during disasters. By integrating local renewable sources like solar or wind with battery storage, communities can maintain power even when centralized infrastructure fails. This decentralized approach accelerates the clean energy transition while strengthening rural and remote energy security globally.
learn.c1_text: A microgrid is a small-scale power system that connects local energy sources—like rooftop solar panels or wind turbines—to nearby homes and businesses. Think of it like a mini electricity grid serving a neighborhood, school, or hospital. Unlike the national grid, a microgrid can 'island' itself during outages, continuing to supply power autonomously using local generation and storage resources.
learn.c2_text: During hurricanes, floods, or wildfires, microgrids keep critical facilities such as hospitals and emergency centers powered. For example, after Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, several microgrids restored electricity within days instead of months. These systems combine smart controls, renewable energy, and batteries to balance supply and demand dynamically, ensuring reliable and adaptive local energy distribution.
learn.c3_text: India has over 500 operational microgrids, primarily in remote areas of states like Bihar, Odisha, and Rajasthan. The government’s Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) program supports off-grid solutions to electrify underserved communities. Companies like Husk Power Systems and Tata Power are deploying solar microgrids to provide 24x7 clean energy access to rural households and small enterprises.
learn.stat1: Over 500 operational microgrids in India as of 2023
learn.stat2: Microgrids can restore power in as little as 24 hours post-disaster
learn.stat3: More than 150 microgrid projects deployed globally since 2020
learn.stat4: Solar microgrids reduce diesel generator usage by up to 70%

learn.title: Floating Solar Farms on Water
learn.intro: Floating solar farms, also known as floatovoltaics, are transforming how we harness sunlight by placing panels directly on reservoirs, lakes, and lagoons. These installations not only generate clean electricity but also reduce water evaporation—a crucial benefit in drought-prone regions. With growing demand for land-efficient renewables, floating PV offers an innovative dual-use solution that supports both energy and water sustainability.
learn.c1_text: Placing solar panels on water surfaces conserves land and boosts efficiency. Cool water beneath the panels reduces panel temperature, increasing output by up to 10%. Additionally, floating arrays minimize evaporation from water bodies—critical in arid climates. Anchored securely, these systems avoid land-use conflicts and can coexist with aquaculture or recreational activities below.
learn.c2_text: Floating solar installations significantly cut water loss through evaporation. In California alone, floating PV on irrigation canals could save billions of gallons annually. A study estimated that covering just 25% of California’s canal network with solar panels would prevent around 100,000 acre-feet of water loss each year, supporting agricultural needs and ecosystem health.
learn.c3_text: India ranks third globally in floating solar capacity with over 1.5 GW installed by 2023. The National Institute of Wind Energy leads development under the Solar Energy Corporation of India’s guidance. Major projects include the 150 MW Ramagundam plant in Telangana and 100 MW Kayamkulam facility in Kerala, targeting 40 GW of floating solar potential nationwide.
learn.stat1: India has over 1.5 GW of floating solar installed as of 2023
learn.stat2: Floating panels can increase efficiency by up to 10% due to cooling
learn.stat3: Globally, over 13 GW of floating solar was installed by 2023
learn.stat4: Covering 25% of California’s canals saves about 100,000 acre-feet of water yearly

learn.title: Geothermal Energy Fundamentals
learn.intro: Geothermal energy taps into the Earth’s internal heat to produce electricity and provide direct heating for homes and industries. Unlike intermittent renewables like solar and wind, geothermal delivers consistent baseload power around the clock. As countries seek reliable clean energy alternatives, geothermal presents a stable, low-carbon option—especially in tectonically active regions where underground heat is abundant and accessible.
learn.c1_text: Deep beneath our feet, the Earth generates enormous amounts of heat from radioactive decay and primordial sources. Geothermal power plants tap into underground steam or hot water reservoirs to spin turbines and generate electricity. Enhanced geothermal systems inject water into hot dry rock to create artificial reservoirs, expanding usable geothermal resources beyond natural hotspots.
learn.c2_text: Geothermal serves two main purposes: electricity generation and direct-use heating. In Iceland, over 90% of homes use geothermal for space and water heating. Electricity production typically requires high-temperature resources found near volcanic zones, while lower-temperature sources can directly heat greenhouses, fish farms, or district heating networks in colder climates.
learn.c3_text: India has identified 342 geothermal prospects across states like Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Himachal Pradesh. The Ministry of Renewable Energy promotes geothermal research through the National Geothermal Programme. Though commercial-scale adoption lags, pilot projects in Tattapani and Manikaran show promise for future expansion using enhanced geothermal technologies.
learn.stat1: Iceland generates over 25% of its electricity from geothermal
learn.stat2: The US leads global geothermal production with over 3.7 GW online
learn.stat3: India has identified 342 geothermal prospects as of 2023
learn.stat4: Geothermal provides constant baseload power unlike solar or wind

learn.title: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) Technology
learn.intro: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology enables electric vehicles to act as mobile energy storage units, feeding electricity back into the power grid when needed. As EV adoption surges, V2G transforms parked cars into dynamic assets that stabilize supply-demand imbalances. This bidirectional energy flow enhances grid flexibility and supports higher penetration of variable renewables like wind and solar.
learn.c1_text: An electric vehicle equipped with bidirectional charging can both draw power from and send power back to the grid. During peak demand or low renewable output, EVs discharge stored energy to support grid stability. Smart software manages timing and pricing, allowing drivers to earn revenue while contributing excess battery capacity to utility-scale balancing services.
learn.c2_text: V2G helps manage short-term fluctuations in electricity supply and demand. With millions of EVs potentially connected, aggregated fleets can provide gigawatts of flexible capacity. For instance, a Nissan Leaf with a 62 kWh battery could supply up to 6 kW of power back to the grid, helping prevent blackouts and defer costly substation upgrades.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 30% EV penetration by 2030 under the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme. While V2G infrastructure remains nascent, pilot studies by IIT Madras explore integrating EVs into smart grids. Policy frameworks are evolving to enable two-way energy flows and incentivize EV owners for grid support services.
learn.stat1: Over 2 million EVs globally capable of V2G by 2023
learn.stat2: A typical EV battery stores 50–100 kWh of usable energy
learn.stat3: Aggregated V2G fleets could provide over 10 GW of grid flexibility
learn.stat4: India targets 30% EV adoption by 2030 under FAME-II

learn.title: Green Hydrogen Production Methods
learn.intro: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, offering a clean fuel alternative for hard-to-decarbonize sectors like steelmaking, shipping, and aviation. Two dominant electrolysis methods—proton exchange membrane (PEM) and alkaline—are shaping the emerging hydrogen economy. Each has distinct advantages depending on scale, cost, and application, making them vital tools in the global shift toward net-zero emissions.
learn.c1_text: Alkaline electrolyzers are cheaper per kilowatt and suited for steady, utility-scale production. They run efficiently for long durations but respond slowly to variable inputs. PEM units cost more initially but adapt quickly to fluctuating power—perfect for pairing with solar/wind farms. Their higher purity output also suits sensitive industrial processes and fuel cell vehicles directly.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2021, India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MMT annual production by 2030. It plans $2.3 billion investment in manufacturing hubs for electrolyzers. Strategic locations like Gujarat and Tamil Nadu will host mega-projects leveraging abundant solar and wind resources. The mission seeks to position India among top three global hydrogen exporters by 2030.
learn.stat1: India targets 5 million metric tons of green hydrogen annually by 2030
learn.stat2: PEM electrolyzers respond within seconds to power changes
learn.stat3: Alkaline systems dominate 70% of global electrolyzer installations
learn.stat4: Global green hydrogen demand expected to reach 50 million tons by 2050

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)
learn.intro: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) uses mirrors or lenses to focus sunlight onto a small area, generating intense heat that drives turbines to produce electricity. Unlike photovoltaic panels, CSP can store thermal energy for hours or days, delivering reliable power even after sunset. This dispatchable solar technology plays a key role in decarbonizing grids requiring consistent, large-scale renewable generation.
learn.c1_text: CSP plants use fields of mirrors called heliostats to reflect and concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver atop a tower. The concentrated light heats a transfer fluid—often molten salt—to over 500°C. This heat generates steam that spins a turbine connected to a generator, producing electricity similar to conventional power plants but powered entirely by sunlight.
learn.c2_text: One major advantage of CSP is built-in thermal storage. Molten salt retains heat for up to 15 hours, allowing electricity generation during peak evening demand or cloudy periods. This makes CSP uniquely valuable compared to solar PV, which stops producing once the sun sets unless paired with expensive external batteries. Storage increases capacity factors to over 50%.
learn.c3_text: India has commissioned over 200 MW of CSP capacity under the National Solar Mission. Notable projects include the 125 MW Shorumpur plant in Rajasthan and 100 MW Dhursar facility. The government plans additional tenders to scale up CSP deployment, emphasizing hybrid models combining CSP with storage to meet evening peak load requirements efficiently.
learn.stat1: India has over 200 MW of operational CSP capacity as of 2023
learn.stat2: CSP with thermal storage can deliver power for up to 15 hours
learn.stat3: Global CSP capacity exceeds 6 GW as of 2023
learn.stat4: CSP can achieve capacity factors above 50%, surpassing solar PV without storage
